title: Estou a falar — the European Portuguese "-ing" form
title_target: O que é que estás a fazer?
goal: Say what's happening right now using the structure used in Portugal — which differs from Brazil — and then sort out *já*, *ainda* and *já não*, which all feel like "already" and "yet".
bekal: telling apart four *já / ainda* combinations that are easily mixed up

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Ao telefone
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost again, this time on the slopes of Bica. He calls Ana.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ana? Sou eu, o Budi. Estás ocupada?
lines.id: Ana? It's me, Budi. Are you busy?
lines.literal: Ana? am I, the Budi. you-are busy?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: I'm having dinner. But go ahead.

lines.text: Não faz mal, estou só a acabar a sopa. O que se passa?

notes: **Estou? is how you answer the phone in Portugal.** Literally "I am?" — roughly "I'm here?". The full form is *Estou sim?*. In Brazil people answer *Alô?*, which sounds foreign in Portugal. To say who you are: *Sou eu, o Budi* or *É o Budi.*

**Estar a + infinitive** is the "-ing" form in Portugal. In Brazil it's *estar* + *-ndo*: *estou falando*. Both are understood in both countries, but only the first sounds natural in Lisbon. It's the second giveaway — after pronoun placement in unit 12 — that tells people fastest where you learned your Portuguese.

**Ligar means to phone in Portugal**, and also "to switch on" (*liga a luz* — turn on the light). *Telefonar* is still correct and slightly more formal. Note that both use the preposition *a* for the person: *ligo-te*, *telefono à Ana*.

**O que se passa?** = "what's up?" or "what's wrong?". Another subjectless structure, like *janta-se* in unit 9. Other ways to say the same thing: *O que é que se passa?* and, more casually, *Que foi?*

**Está um elétrico a passar** — notice that *estar a* works for things too, not just people, and that the subject can come **after** the verb. This order is typical for introducing something that has just come into view, like English "there's a tram going past".
**Pois estou** — answering by repeating the verb, a habit you've seen since unit 1. Adding *pois* gives it a feel of "oh, right, so I am".

grammars.title: Estar a + infinitive
body: The structure never changes: the right form of *estar*, then *a*, then the verb in its infinitive form, which never changes.
after: **This form is less common than you'd think.** Portuguese uses the simple present for many things that need "-ing" in English: *Trabalho num banco* (I work / I'm working at a bank), *Moro em Lisboa* (I live in Lisbon). Use *estar a* only when the action is truly **happening at that very moment**.
To negate, *não* stays in front of *estar*: *Não estou a perceber* — a sentence you'll use a lot in Portugal, and gentler than *não percebo*.
If there's an object pronoun, it attaches to the infinitive: *Estou a ver-te* — or, if there's a puller, jumps to the front of the whole structure: *Não te estou a ver.*

grammars.title: Other verbs that take a + infinitive
body: The same *a* + infinitive pattern works with several other verbs, all of them very common.
after: **Voltar a + infinitive** is how Portuguese says "again": *voltar a ver* = to see again, *voltar a ler* = to read again. English puts "again" at the end; Portuguese adds it as an extra verb in front.
**Andar a + infinitive** is typical of Portugal and has no neat equivalent: it means something that has been going on for a while lately. *Ando a pensar nisso* = "I've been thinking about it lately".

grammars.title: Já, ainda, ainda não, já não
body: Four combinations that handle "already", "still" and "not yet". The differences are sharp.
after: **Já não is the one most often missed.** It describes something that **used to be true and has stopped**: *já não fumo* (I don't smoke anymore), *já não trabalho lá* (I don't work there anymore). Saying *não já* is always wrong.
*Já* on its own also means "right away" or "in a moment": *Vou já!* = "I'm coming right now", *Já venho* = "I'll be right back".

blocks.text: Phone numbers in Portugal are given **in groups**: 912 345 678 is read *nove-um-dois, três-quatro-cinco, seis-sete-oito* or, more often, *novecentos e doze, trezentos e quarenta e cinco, seiscentos e setenta e oito*. If in doubt, reading the digits one by one is still understood.

blocks.title: Portugal vs. Brazil at a glance
items: "I'm speaking": Portugal *estou a falar* — Brazil *estou falando*.
Mobile phone: Portugal *o telemóvel* — Brazil *o celular*.
All of these come up in first-day conversations, so these are the differences most worth remembering if your learning materials are mixed.

exercises.prompt: Change into the "-ing" form with estar a.
Fill in já, ainda, ainda não or já não.
items: ____ estou a comer, espera um pouco.
Ele ____ trabalha aqui, saiu no ano passado.
